title: Mixtures, Solutions and Separation
scope_note: Class IX concepts, with experimental inference enrichment as indicated
introduction: Understanding a mixture means more than naming a separation technique. This chapter moves from substance identity and dispersed phases through concentration and solubility to experimental designs that recover components. It teaches the property difference that makes each separation possible.

subtopics.title: Elements, compounds and mixtures
subtopics.entry_question: Salt water is transparent, and so is pure water. Are they chemically the same kind of matter?
core1a_paragraphs: An element consists of one chemical element; a compound contains chemically joined elements in a characteristic composition; a mixture combines substances without a fixed chemical combination ratio. Appearance alone cannot tell us which category we have.

A pure sample of sodium chloride is a compound represented by NaCl. Salt water is a mixture of water and dissolved NaCl, with variable concentration. Changing the amount of salt alters the mixture's composition without changing the chemical formula of either component.

Separation method is evidence: a physical process such as evaporation can recover salt from a salt solution. Decomposing the chemical compound NaCl into sodium and chlorine is a different type of transformation and cannot be achieved by ordinary evaporation.
subtopics.representation: Compare particle diagrams: pure element A; pure compound AB with all units identical; mixture of independent A and B species. Do not draw dissolved salt as undissociated NaCl molecules by default; aqueous Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are present.

worked_example.problem: Classify copper metal, pure water and salt water.
steps: Copper consists of atoms of one element: element.
Pure H₂O has characteristic combination of hydrogen and oxygen: compound.
Salt water has variable proportions of at least two substances: mixture.
worked_example.check: Try adjusting salt concentration: mixture changes continuously, but H₂O stays H₂O.

misconception.wrong: Anything transparent and uniform must be a pure compound.
misconception.why: A homogeneous mixture can look identical to a pure liquid.
misconception.repair: Use composition variability and separability, not only visual uniformity.

demands.title: Composition versus chemical identity
demands.core1a_explanation: Composition is fixed for a pure compound but variable for mixtures; connect that distinction to recoverability of components.
demands.worked_reasoning: Adding 5 g salt to 100 g water and adding 20 g salt to 100 g water can produce different mixtures, not new formulas for NaCl.
demands.independent_check: Distinguish component formula from mixture proportions.
hints: Name the relevant chemical species and the observed state.
Check which property distinguishes the candidate explanations.
Conserve each component while changing a condition; do not assume the conclusion.

core1b.predict: Make an initial classification or qualitative prediction and state one condition it depends upon.
core1b.attempt: Why can a salt solution have different salt percentages without changing the chemical identity of salt?
core1b.reconstruct: Rebuild the solution by comparing each candidate model against the observations and conservation rules.
core1b.diagnose: Which observation would expose the incorrect route: Changing percentage changes the chemical formula of salt?
core1b.repair: Keep species identities separate from relative amounts.
core1b.boundary: Would varying the ratio of hydrogen to oxygen in pure water create a different pure water formula?
core1b.model_response: The solution is a mixture with adjustable relative amounts. Dissolved salt provides Na⁺/Cl⁻; the compound's ionic formula remains NaCl, representing a fixed ratio of its ions.

demands.title: Particle diagram classification
demands.core1a_explanation: A particle model must preserve whether unlike atoms are connected into repeated compound units or coexist as different substances.
demands.worked_reasoning: For a molecular compound A₂B, depict identical A₂B groups; for a mixture depict A₂B and C groups separated without forced connectivity.
demands.independent_check: Check all particle identities in a diagram.
hints: Name the relevant chemical species and the observed state.
Check which property distinguishes the candidate explanations.
Conserve each component while changing a condition; do not assume the conclusion.

core1b.predict: Make an initial classification or qualitative prediction and state one condition it depends upon.
core1b.attempt: A box contains identical AB molecules and free B₂ molecules. Is it an element, compound or mixture? Explain the model.
core1b.reconstruct: Rebuild the solution by comparing each candidate model against the observations and conservation rules.
core1b.diagnose: Which observation would expose the incorrect route: Presence of bonds automatically makes the whole sample a compound?
core1b.repair: Count distinct chemical species, not just bond marks.
core1b.boundary: Would the answer change if all B₂ were removed?
core1b.model_response: Mixture: two distinct substances AB and B₂ coexist. Some particles are bonded, but there is more than one substance in the box.

demands.title: Multiple observations and purity
demands.core1a_explanation: Homogeneity, boiling behaviour and separation can constrain identity without uniquely resolving every component.
demands.worked_reasoning: A transparent sample yields a solid residue after water evaporates; this supports a nonvolatile solute in a mixture, not a new pure water compound.
demands.independent_check: State uncertainty after classifying.
hints: Name the relevant chemical species and the observed state.
Check which property distinguishes the candidate explanations.
Conserve each component while changing a condition; do not assume the conclusion.

core1b.predict: Make an initial classification or qualitative prediction and state one condition it depends upon.
core1b.attempt: An unknown transparent liquid leaves white crystals when evaporated and its composition varies between batches. Construct the strongest justified classification.
core1b.reconstruct: Rebuild the solution by comparing each candidate model against the observations and conservation rules.
core1b.diagnose: Which observation would expose the incorrect route: One crystallisation proves the exact chemical name of the solute?
core1b.repair: Separate classification from identification and propose a confirmatory test.
core1b.boundary: Could multiple dissolved solutes crystallise together?
core1b.model_response: It is consistent with a homogeneous mixture of a volatile liquid and nonvolatile solute, not a pure single compound. Identify the recovered solid and test composition before naming it.

subtopics.source_notes: Class IX pure substances and mixtures.

deep_dive.big_idea: A transparent liquid may be pure, or it may conceal several substances uniformly mixed together. Chemical identity does not come from colour or clarity. It comes from the species present and whether their relative amounts are intrinsic to one compound or adjustable as mixture composition.
reasoning_path: Define the proposed sample: pure H₂O has fixed molecular identity, while salt solution contains water and dissolved ionic species.
Ask whether changing the concentration changes the formula of the solute; it does not.
Identify a physical property that permits separation without turning the components into new chemical substances.
Account for products in each stage. Recovering a component does not prove the starting mixture contained only that component.

discovery.title: Different salt mixtures, same salt
discovery.setup: Imagine two flasks with equal water mass but different amounts of dissolved NaCl. Compare a controlled evaporation-and-recovery model.
discovery.predict: If one flask has twice as much dissolved salt, must its dissolved formula change from NaCl to Na₂Cl?
discovery.observation: The recovered salt amount differs but its representative ionic formula unit remains NaCl, assuming no reaction or contamination.
discovery.interpretation: A mixture can vary in composition while a constituent compound retains chemical identity.
discovery.limits: Recovered material may contain impurities; chemical identity cannot be certified solely by white crystalline appearance.

deep_dive.connection: Mixture composition leads to the next question: at what scale does a sample appear uniform?

subtopics.title: Homogeneous and heterogeneous systems
subtopics.entry_question: If no particles are visible in a milk sample, does that make it homogeneous at every scale?
core1a_paragraphs: A homogeneous mixture appears compositionally uniform at the relevant observation scale; a heterogeneous mixture has distinguishable regions or phases. 'Homogeneous' is not a claim that all particles are literally identical.

Salt completely dissolved in water forms an apparently uniform solution. Muddy water has suspended particles that can vary between sampled regions. Milk may appear uniform to the eye while containing dispersed droplets at smaller scales, making scale important.
Mixing and settling can change whether an initially dispersed sample remains uniform. A classification should declare the observation scale, sampling method and time after preparation.
subtopics.representation: Show three magnification levels: visible glass, microscopic suspended droplets, molecular-scale dissolved ions. Label the scale, not only the apparent colour.

worked_example.problem: Compare salt solution and sand stirred into water after leaving both to rest.
steps: Salt remains dispersed as solvated components at ordinary concentrations.
Sand remains as separate solid grains and typically settles.
Salt water is homogeneous at ordinary observation scale; sand water is heterogeneous.
worked_example.check: Inspect different positions and wait for settling.

misconception.wrong: A mixture that looks uniform for one second is a permanently homogeneous solution.
misconception.why: Fine suspensions can appear uniform briefly.
misconception.repair: Repeat sampling over time and at an appropriate scale.

demands.title: Observation scale matters
demands.core1a_explanation: Explain how visible uniformity and microscopic heterogeneity can coexist.
demands.worked_reasoning: Milk disperses fat droplets within a water-rich phase; the sample appears uniform to the naked eye but is not a molecular solution.
demands.independent_check: Distinguish appearance from composition.
hints: Name the relevant chemical species and the observed state.
Check which property distinguishes the candidate explanations.
Conserve each component while changing a condition; do not assume the conclusion.

core1b.predict: Make an initial classification or qualitative prediction and state one condition it depends upon.
core1b.attempt: Why can milk look homogeneous but be described as a colloid?
core1b.reconstruct: Rebuild the solution by comparing each candidate model against the observations and conservation rules.
core1b.diagnose: Which observation would expose the incorrect route: Uniform appearance proves only one chemical species is present?
core1b.repair: Specify scale and dispersed-phase model.
core1b.boundary: Would a microscope or light-scattering test yield new information?
core1b.model_response: Its droplet-scale dispersed phase may be too small to resolve by eye, while its microscopic structure has two phases. Classification depends on scale and particle behaviour.

demands.title: Model solutions and suspensions
demands.core1a_explanation: A particle diagram should represent both size regime and whether a dispersed species remains stable over time.
demands.worked_reasoning: A solution sketch uses molecular/ionic solutes; a suspension sketch uses comparatively large solid particles with settling tendency.
demands.independent_check: Test whether 'smaller' automatically means 'dissolved'.
hints: Name the relevant chemical species and the observed state.
Check which property distinguishes the candidate explanations.
Conserve each component while changing a condition; do not assume the conclusion.

core1b.predict: Make an initial classification or qualitative prediction and state one condition it depends upon.
core1b.attempt: Describe two particle models for salt water and fine chalk in water.
core1b.reconstruct: Rebuild the solution by comparing each candidate model against the observations and conservation rules.
core1b.diagnose: Which observation would expose the incorrect route: All white particles in water are molecular solutes?
core1b.repair: Identify solid particles versus dissolved species.
core1b.boundary: What if the chalk were ground into smaller particles?
core1b.model_response: Salt water contains dispersed hydrated ions; chalk remains as suspended solid particles and may settle. The models differ in size and dissolution, not simply 'white versus clear'.

demands.title: Infer mixture class from multiple tests
demands.core1a_explanation: Decide classification using settling, transparency and light scattering together.
demands.worked_reasoning: A cloudy sample scatters a beam and does not settle quickly; a colloid is plausible, whereas a coarse suspension might settle.
demands.independent_check: Multiple observations must constrain the classification.
hints: Name the relevant chemical species and the observed state.
Check which property distinguishes the candidate explanations.
Conserve each component while changing a condition; do not assume the conclusion.

core1b.predict: Make an initial classification or qualitative prediction and state one condition it depends upon.
core1b.attempt: A dispersal stays cloudy for hours, strongly scatters light and passes through ordinary filter paper. Is it certainly a true molecular solution?
core1b.reconstruct: Rebuild the solution by comparing each candidate model against the observations and conservation rules.
core1b.diagnose: Which observation would expose the incorrect route: Anything passing filter paper must be truly dissolved?
core1b.repair: Combine scattering, stability and separation evidence.
core1b.boundary: Would ultrafiltration provide a stronger discriminating test?
core1b.model_response: No. These observations are compatible with a colloid of particles smaller than ordinary filter-paper pores. Scattering opposes the simple true-solution classification; additional particle-size evidence may help.

subtopics.source_notes: Class IX mixtures and dispersed systems.

deep_dive.big_idea: Homogeneity is partly a question of scale and time. A fine dispersion can look uniform to the naked eye while containing droplets or solid particles that microscopy reveals. Chemists therefore combine appearance with tests of settling, scattering and microscopic structure.
reasoning_path: Describe what an observer sees at a stated scale and after a stated time.
Test whether samples from different regions have the same composition; a temporarily stirred suspension may fail on standing.
Distinguish a molecular/ionic solution from colloids with dispersed particles and suspensions that often settle.
Reconsider whether filtration would work based on size and phase, not just on whether the liquid looks cloudy.

discovery.title: The cloudy-versus-clear comparison
discovery.setup: Consider salt solution, well-stirred chalk suspension and a stable milk-like colloid as three labelled models, not real samples to consume.
discovery.predict: Which sample is likely to settle, which may scatter a beam without settling quickly, and which retains dissolved ions?
discovery.observation: A coarse chalk suspension often settles; colloidal droplets may persist and scatter light; salt ions stay dissolved at suitable conditions.
discovery.interpretation: Several independent observations are needed because appearance at one scale does not uniquely establish microscopic structure.
discovery.limits: Real suspensions differ in concentration, particle size and aggregation; classifications are practical ranges rather than magical thresholds.

deep_dive.connection: The same distinctions will guide light-scattering and filtration measurements.

subtopics.title: Solutions, suspensions and colloids
subtopics.entry_question: Why can a transparent salt solution and a cloudy colloid both resist ordinary settling?
core1a_paragraphs: A true solution has solute present at molecular or ionic scale. In a suspension, larger particles remain distinct from the medium and can settle. A colloid contains dispersed particles intermediate in behaviour; many remain stable for long periods but scatter light.

The Tyndall effect arises from scattering of light by particles or droplets in an appropriate size range. It is one clue, not a universal on/off detector without specifying concentration, wavelength and experimental geometry.

Filtration with ordinary filter paper separates many suspensions but generally does not remove truly dissolved solutes. Some colloids also pass ordinary filters; their separation can require different methods.
subtopics.representation: Compare (a) transparent salt solution with ions, (b) stable colloid with droplets causing a visible beam and (c) suspension with larger grains and settling.

worked_example.problem: A liquid scatters a narrow beam of light and remains uniform for hours. Which classification is plausible?
steps: Light scattering indicates dispersed structures capable of redirecting light.
Long-term stability weighs against a coarse rapidly settling suspension.
The evidence supports a colloidal dispersion.
A single observation does not identify the particles' chemical nature.
worked_example.result: Colloid is plausible; composition not uniquely identified.
worked_example.check: Compare ordinary filtration and microscopic size evidence.

misconception.wrong: A visible beam in any liquid proves a chemical reaction is occurring.
misconception.why: Light scattering is a physical optical effect of dispersed particles.
misconception.repair: Separate optical observations from species-changing reactions.

demands.title: Scattering without chemical change
demands.core1a_explanation: Connect light interacting with dispersed particles to a visible beam.
demands.worked_reasoning: A colloid may show a visible beam because dispersed droplets scatter incoming light toward the observer.
demands.independent_check: Use a scattering mechanism in the correct medium.
hints: Name the relevant chemical species and the observed state.
Check which property distinguishes the candidate explanations.
Conserve each component while changing a condition; do not assume the conclusion.

core1b.predict: Make an initial classification or qualitative prediction and state one condition it depends upon.
core1b.attempt: Why can a foggy medium show a light beam more clearly than clean air?
core1b.reconstruct: Rebuild the solution by comparing each candidate model against the observations and conservation rules.
core1b.diagnose: Which observation would expose the incorrect route: A visible beam means light energy causes droplet formation?
core1b.repair: Separate scattering of existing droplets from their production.
core1b.boundary: Would the beam look as distinct in particle-free air?
core1b.model_response: Water droplets scatter light toward the observer. The stronger visible beam can arise from dispersion without making a new chemical species.

demands.title: Choose between true solution and colloid
demands.core1a_explanation: A particle-size/dispersed-phase model is needed in addition to transparency.
demands.worked_reasoning: Sugar dissolved in water yields molecular solute; milk contains colloidal droplets.
demands.independent_check: State measurement conditions.
hints: Name the relevant chemical species and the observed state.
Check which property distinguishes the candidate explanations.
Conserve each component while changing a condition; do not assume the conclusion.

core1b.predict: Make an initial classification or qualitative prediction and state one condition it depends upon.
core1b.attempt: A stable sample looks uniform but scatters light strongly. Which model is better: molecular solution or colloid?
core1b.reconstruct: Rebuild the solution by comparing each candidate model against the observations and conservation rules.
core1b.diagnose: Which observation would expose the incorrect route: Anything uniform to eye is a true solution?
core1b.repair: Use optical and separation evidence before classification.
core1b.boundary: Would diluting the sample affect scattering intensity?
core1b.model_response: A colloidal dispersion is more consistent, subject to control of instrument and concentration; a single beam is not an absolute test.

demands.title: Combine filter and scattering tests
demands.core1a_explanation: A decision should integrate multiple experimental criteria without overclaiming identity.
demands.worked_reasoning: Passing ordinary filter paper and scattering a beam can indicate a colloid smaller than filter pores.
demands.independent_check: Acknowledge ambiguous boundary cases.
hints: Name the relevant chemical species and the observed state.
Check which property distinguishes the candidate explanations.
Conserve each component while changing a condition; do not assume the conclusion.

core1b.predict: Make an initial classification or qualitative prediction and state one condition it depends upon.
core1b.attempt: Liquid X passes filter paper, does not settle in two days and shows pronounced Tyndall scattering. What can we infer and what remains unknown?
core1b.reconstruct: Rebuild the solution by comparing each candidate model against the observations and conservation rules.
core1b.diagnose: Which observation would expose the incorrect route: Filtration passage rules out dispersed particles?
core1b.repair: Explain filter pore limitations and recommend a size-sensitive method.
core1b.boundary: Could some dyes or large molecules complicate the optical conclusion?
core1b.model_response: A colloid is plausible. The dispersed chemical identity and precise size remain unknown; ordinary filtration and stability do not establish a true solution.

deep_dive.big_idea: A dispersed sample must be classified by the state and size of its distributed components, not simply whether it resembles a solution in a photograph. Colloids can remain stable for long periods while scattering light; solutions have molecular or ionic-scale solute, and ordinary suspensions have larger particles.
reasoning_path: Use a particle-scale representation to decide whether the dispersed entities are dissolved species or separate particles.
Test optical scattering under controlled lighting; a visible beam can be evidence of a dispersed phase but is sensitive to concentration.
Test settling and ordinary filtration. Remember that passing ordinary filter paper does not guarantee molecular dissolution.
State what the experiment cannot conclude: scattering does not uniquely identify the chemical species or prove purity.

discovery.title: A three-test classification
discovery.setup: A sample scatters a narrow beam of light, passes ordinary filter paper and remains apparently uniform overnight.
discovery.predict: Is a true molecular solution established by these observations?
discovery.observation: The combination is consistent with some stable colloidal dispersions whose particles are smaller than filter-paper pores.
discovery.interpretation: Light scattering and dispersion stability suggest a colloidal model, but particle size and identity remain to be measured.
discovery.limits: Concentration, wavelength, sample colour and instrument geometry can influence visible scattering.

deep_dive.connection: To compare two solutions quantitatively, the next lesson defines concentration with an explicit denominator.

subtopics.title: Concentration: mass/mass, mass/volume, volume/volume
subtopics.entry_question: Two drinks both contain 10 g sugar, but one is a cup and the other a litre. Which is more concentrated?
core1a_paragraphs: Concentration expresses an amount of solute relative to a specified quantity of mixture or solution. The denominator is essential: mass fraction uses total solution mass, whereas mass/volume concentration uses solution volume.
Ten grams sugar in 100 g solution is 10% by mass. Ten grams in 100 mL solution is 10 g per 100 mL, often written 10% m/V. These measures are not interchangeable without density information.

Dilution adds solvent while preserving the amount of nonreacting solute in the ideal model. Concentration decreases because the denominator rises; pouring away part of a well-mixed solution changes solute amount and total volume proportionally but leaves concentration unchanged.
subtopics.representation: Use a ratio bar with numerator solute mass and denominator total solution mass or volume. Explicitly label % m/m or % m/V and do not substitute solvent mass.

worked_example.problem: A 120 g solution contains 18 g solute. Calculate mass percentage.
steps: Use mass fraction = solute mass / total solution mass.
Substitute 18 g / 120 g = 0.15.
Multiply by 100 to obtain percent.
worked_example.check: 18 g solute + 102 g solvent = 120 g solution.

misconception.wrong: Use only solvent mass in the denominator for mass percentage.
misconception.why: The defined mass percentage uses total solution mass.
misconception.repair: Write the concentration definition and units before substituting.

demands.title: Track concentration under dilution
demands.core1a_explanation: Adding solvent changes total solution amount but not the mass of retained nonreacting solute.
demands.worked_reasoning: 20 g solute in 200 g solution is 10% m/m; adding 200 g water makes 400 g total at 5% m/m.
demands.independent_check: Check the numerator conserved before removing any solution.
hints: Name the relevant chemical species and the observed state.
Check which property distinguishes the candidate explanations.
Conserve each component while changing a condition; do not assume the conclusion.

core1b.predict: Make an initial classification or qualitative prediction and state one condition it depends upon.
core1b.attempt: A 300 g solution contains 30 g dissolved salt. After adding 200 g water, what is its mass percent, assuming no loss?
core1b.reconstruct: Rebuild the solution by comparing each candidate model against the observations and conservation rules.
core1b.diagnose: Which observation would expose the incorrect route: Dilution creates or destroys solute?
core1b.repair: Write a solute-mass conservation ledger.
core1b.boundary: If 100 g of well-mixed diluted solution is removed, what is concentration of remainder?
core1b.model_response: Salt remains 30 g; total mass becomes 500 g; mass fraction = 30/500 ×100 = 6%.

demands.title: Choose the right denominator
demands.core1a_explanation: Different percentage labels represent different physical ratios; a unit tag is part of meaning.
demands.worked_reasoning: 10% m/m means 10 g per 100 g solution; 10% m/V means 10 g per 100 mL solution.
demands.independent_check: Interpret units, not just numbers.
hints: Name the relevant chemical species and the observed state.
Check which property distinguishes the candidate explanations.
Conserve each component while changing a condition; do not assume the conclusion.

core1b.predict: Make an initial classification or qualitative prediction and state one condition it depends upon.
core1b.attempt: A label says '5% m/V'. Explain what can be asserted about solute and solution, and why this is not 5% m/m.
core1b.reconstruct: Rebuild the solution by comparing each candidate model against the observations and conservation rules.
core1b.diagnose: Which observation would expose the incorrect route: Every percentage uses identical denominator?
core1b.repair: Carry units through the fraction.
core1b.boundary: How would solution density support conversion between % m/V and % m/m?
core1b.model_response: It denotes 5 g solute per 100 mL solution (at defined conditions). Without solution density one cannot convert confidently to g per 100 g solution.

demands.title: Mass balance in concentration changes
demands.core1a_explanation: Mixing two solutions conserves solute mass under nonreacting assumptions; masses combine even when volumes may not.
demands.worked_reasoning: 100 g of 10% salt solution contains 10 g salt; 100 g of 20% contains 20 g, yielding 30 g in 200 g, or 15%.
demands.independent_check: Independent mass ledger and weighted average check.
hints: Name the relevant chemical species and the observed state.
Check which property distinguishes the candidate explanations.
Conserve each component while changing a condition; do not assume the conclusion.

core1b.predict: Make an initial classification or qualitative prediction and state one condition it depends upon.
core1b.attempt: Mix 200 g of 5% m/m sugar solution with 300 g of 15% m/m sugar solution. Find resulting mass percentage.
core1b.reconstruct: Rebuild the solution by comparing each candidate model against the observations and conservation rules.
core1b.diagnose: Which observation would expose the incorrect route: Average 5% and 15% without weighting by masses?
core1b.repair: Compute individual solute masses before combining.
core1b.boundary: Would a simple arithmetic average work if both solution masses were equal?
core1b.model_response: First contributes 10 g sugar; second 45 g. Total sugar 55 g, total solution mass 500 g; concentration 11% m/m.

subtopics.source_notes: Class IX concentration with extended multi-mixture reasoning.

deep_dive.big_idea: A concentration value is incomplete unless we say what amount of solute is divided by what amount of mixture or solvent. Ten grams per 100 grams of solution is not the same definition as ten grams per 100 millilitres of solution; percentages cannot be compared blindly when density matters.
reasoning_path: Write concentration as a named ratio before inserting any measured values.
Check whether the denominator is total solution mass, solution volume or solvent amount; each answers a different question.
For dilution with no chemical reaction, conserve the actual solute quantity while updating the solution amount.
For mixing, combine actual solute masses first and only then calculate the new concentration; unweighted averages generally fail for unequal masses.

discovery.title: Two bottles, the same percentage sign
discovery.setup: Bottle A reads 10% m/m and bottle B reads 10% m/V. No density is supplied.
discovery.predict: Can we assert the two liquids contain equal masses of solute per equal mass of solution?
discovery.observation: A specifies 10 g solute per 100 g solution; B specifies 10 g per 100 mL solution.
discovery.interpretation: Unit-labelled denominators carry scientific meaning; converting between them requires additional density data.
discovery.limits: Percent concentration arithmetic assumes appropriate mixing behaviour and explicitly stated mass/volume bases.

deep_dive.connection: A concentrated sample may still be unsaturated; solubility introduces a new equilibrium constraint.

subtopics.title: Solubility versus temperature
subtopics.entry_question: Why does heating water usually dissolve more sugar, but a dissolved gas may escape more readily?
core1a_paragraphs: Solubility is the maximum amount of a solute that can dissolve in a given amount of solvent at stated conditions and at equilibrium. The dissolved amount in an unsaturated sample can be smaller than its solubility.

For many solids in water, solubility increases with temperature; this is not universal. Gas solubility often decreases as temperature increases at fixed gas partial pressure. The actual direction depends on the substance and conditions.

Crystallisation can result when a hot saturated solution cools. An experimental calculation must specify whether solvent mass is conserved and whether the excess solute crystallises completely at equilibrium.
subtopics.representation: Draw solubility-versus-temperature curves for a hypothetical solid and gas as illustrative trends, explicitly mark hypothetical and avoid implying every substance follows the same slope.

worked_example.problem: At one temperature, salt solubility is 36 g per 100 g water. How much can dissolve in 250 g water?
steps: Ratio is 36/100 grams solute per gram water.
Multiply by 250 g solvent.
Maximum solute mass = 90 g under same conditions.
worked_example.result: 90 g of that salt can dissolve in 250 g water at the stated temperature.
worked_example.check: 90/250 = 36/100; no mistaken use of solution mass.

misconception.wrong: Solubility always rises when temperature rises.
misconception.why: Different solids and gases may show different temperature dependences.
misconception.repair: Read the specific solute curve and state fixed conditions.

demands.title: Solubility mass-balance
demands.core1a_explanation: A solubility table gives g solute per 100 g solvent, not per 100 g final solution.
demands.worked_reasoning: If maximum dissolvable salt is 40 g per 100 g water, 150 g water can dissolve 60 g at equilibrium.
demands.independent_check: Check total solute conserved.
hints: Name the relevant chemical species and the observed state.
Check which property distinguishes the candidate explanations.
Conserve each component while changing a condition; do not assume the conclusion.

core1b.predict: Make an initial classification or qualitative prediction and state one condition it depends upon.
core1b.attempt: If a salt's solubility is 25 g per 100 g water, how much remains undissolved when 50 g is added to 100 g water at that temperature?
core1b.reconstruct: Rebuild the solution by comparing each candidate model against the observations and conservation rules.
core1b.diagnose: Which observation would expose the incorrect route: 100 g water means 100 g final solution?
core1b.repair: Identify solvent denominator and saturation threshold.
core1b.boundary: What would change with 200 g water?
core1b.model_response: At most 25 g dissolves; 25 g remains undissolved under equilibrium assumptions.

demands.title: Cooling a saturated solution
demands.core1a_explanation: The solubility curve becomes a model for precipitation when temperature changes.
demands.worked_reasoning: A solution saturated at 60°C may contain more dissolved solid than is soluble after cooling, leading to crystals.
demands.independent_check: Check initial dissolved amount against both limits.
hints: Name the relevant chemical species and the observed state.
Check which property distinguishes the candidate explanations.
Conserve each component while changing a condition; do not assume the conclusion.

core1b.predict: Make an initial classification or qualitative prediction and state one condition it depends upon.
core1b.attempt: At 60°C solubility is 60 g/100g water; at 20°C it is 20 g/100g. Cool 100 g water saturated at 60°C. How many grams may crystallise?
core1b.reconstruct: Rebuild the solution by comparing each candidate model against the observations and conservation rules.
core1b.diagnose: Which observation would expose the incorrect route: Cooling always produces the same amount of crystals regardless of initial solution state?
core1b.repair: Check initial saturation and final solvent mass.
core1b.boundary: If the initial solution had only 10 g solute, would anything crystallise?
core1b.model_response: The solution begins with 60 g dissolved; at 20°C only 20 g remains at equilibrium; 40 g crystallises if no solvent is lost.

demands.title: Interpret incomplete solubility data
demands.core1a_explanation: A concentration-versus-temperature experiment may reflect kinetic delay, solvent loss or supersaturation; infer only what is supported.
demands.worked_reasoning: Rapid cooling can delay crystal nucleation, so an apparently clear solution can be temporarily supersaturated.
demands.independent_check: Identify a falsifiable experimental distinction.
hints: Name the relevant chemical species and the observed state.
Check which property distinguishes the candidate explanations.
Conserve each component while changing a condition; do not assume the conclusion.

core1b.predict: Make an initial classification or qualitative prediction and state one condition it depends upon.
core1b.attempt: A solution stays clear after rapid cooling below its equilibrium solubility. Does this disprove the measured solubility curve?
core1b.reconstruct: Rebuild the solution by comparing each candidate model against the observations and conservation rules.
core1b.diagnose: Which observation would expose the incorrect route: A clear solution is always unsaturated?
core1b.repair: Distinguish equilibrium solubility from observed transient state.
core1b.boundary: What would adding a seed crystal test?
core1b.model_response: No. Supersaturation and delayed nucleation are plausible. Disturbance or seeding may induce crystallisation. The observation alone does not overturn equilibrium data.

subtopics.source_notes: Solid and gas solubility conditional trends; supersaturation is extension.

deep_dive.big_idea: The word 'soluble' does not mean infinite solubility. At a given temperature and other stated conditions, a saturated solution is in equilibrium with the undissolved material. The amount that can dissolve depends on the particular substance and sometimes changes strongly with temperature.
reasoning_path: Distinguish the concentration currently present from the maximum equilibrium solubility.
Read the specific curve rather than assuming every solid becomes more soluble when heated.
When cooling a saturated solution, conserve the solute inventory and compare it with the new equilibrium capacity.
If a cooled solution remains clear, consider supersaturation and nucleation delay rather than abandoning conservation.

discovery.title: Cooling the ideal saturated flask
discovery.setup: A model solute dissolves 60 g per 100 g water at a hot temperature but only 20 g per 100 g water at a cold temperature. Solvent mass stays 100 g.
discovery.predict: At equilibrium, how much solid should crystallise when a saturated hot sample is cooled?
discovery.observation: A 40 g reduction in dissolved capacity predicts 40 g solid under the ideal equilibrium model.
discovery.interpretation: Crystallisation follows from a change in solubility at constant solvent inventory.
discovery.limits: Nucleation delay, water evaporation or non-equilibrium cooling may prevent an immediate 40 g visible deposit.

deep_dive.connection: This temperature-dependent separation is an instance of the broader principle of exploiting physical property contrasts.

subtopics.title: Separation: crystallisation, distillation and chromatography
subtopics.entry_question: How can pure water be recovered from salty water without chemically destroying salt?
core1a_paragraphs: Separation depends on differences in physical properties: volatility, solubility, adsorption, particle size and phase behaviour. A successful method targets the relevant difference rather than a familiar equipment name.

Crystallisation can recover dissolved solid while leaving some impurities in solution. Simple distillation heats a solution, collects vapour and condenses it in a separate receiver; nonvolatile salt generally remains behind. Fractional distillation is useful when volatile components have relatively close boiling ranges.

Chromatography separates components that distribute differently between a mobile phase and a stationary phase. Spots appearing at different positions provide evidence of distinct movement, not automatically of chemical purity or unique identity.
subtopics.representation: Diagram a distillation train: heated salt water, vapour path, condenser, receiver, salt residue; arrows follow the path of water only, never salt 'evaporating' with water in the simple model.

worked_example.problem: Choose a method to recover both salt and water from sea-water-like brine.
steps: Identify water as volatile and salt as largely nonvolatile.
Use simple distillation to condense water vapour into a receiving vessel.
Recover salt from concentrated residue by further evaporation/crystallisation.
Check contamination and recovery losses independently.
worked_example.check: Mass ledger for collected water, salt and residue plus apparatus losses.

misconception.wrong: Filtration separates dissolved salt from water.
misconception.why: Ordinary filter pores are vastly larger than dissolved ions and solvent molecules.
misconception.repair: Choose a technique based on dissolved state and property contrasts.

demands.title: Why distillation works
demands.core1a_explanation: The apparatus separates substances by vapour formation and condensation, not by filtering tiny ions.
demands.worked_reasoning: Brine heated to boil produces vapour enriched in water; condenser returns it to liquid separate from nonvolatile salt.
demands.independent_check: Track where each component goes.
hints: Name the relevant chemical species and the observed state.
Check which property distinguishes the candidate explanations.
Conserve each component while changing a condition; do not assume the conclusion.

core1b.predict: Make an initial classification or qualitative prediction and state one condition it depends upon.
core1b.attempt: Why does a condenser in a simple salt-water distillation yield fresh water?
core1b.reconstruct: Rebuild the solution by comparing each candidate model against the observations and conservation rules.
core1b.diagnose: Which observation would expose the incorrect route: Filter paper at the condenser removes the salt ions?
core1b.repair: Identify vapour–liquid transformation and separation path.
core1b.boundary: Could violent boiling contaminate the distillate?
core1b.model_response: Water vaporises and condenses in a separate vessel; the dissolved salt is nonvolatile under the conditions and stays behind. Purity still depends on preventing droplets from being entrained.

demands.title: Chromatogram as composition evidence
demands.core1a_explanation: A chromatogram encodes relative travel distances, not molecular masses directly.
demands.worked_reasoning: A dye spot splits into two after paper chromatography, indicating at least two components with distinguishable migration under the conditions.
demands.independent_check: Use mobile/stationary phase mechanism.
hints: Name the relevant chemical species and the observed state.
Check which property distinguishes the candidate explanations.
Conserve each component while changing a condition; do not assume the conclusion.

core1b.predict: Make an initial classification or qualitative prediction and state one condition it depends upon.
core1b.attempt: A black ink produces blue and yellow spots. What inference is justified and which is not?
core1b.reconstruct: Rebuild the solution by comparing each candidate model against the observations and conservation rules.
core1b.diagnose: Which observation would expose the incorrect route: Same colour or travel distance means identical chemical identity?
core1b.repair: State what was measured and require independent identification evidence.
core1b.boundary: Would changing the solvent alter migration distance?
core1b.model_response: The sample contains components that separate into at least two differently migrating coloured bands under these conditions; exact chemical identity is not established by colour alone.

demands.title: Design a separation sequence
demands.core1a_explanation: Multicomponent mixtures may need more than one property difference and thus more than one stage.
demands.worked_reasoning: Separate insoluble sand by filtration; distil water away from dissolved salt; recover salt by crystallisation.
demands.independent_check: Specify a method for each property contrast.
hints: Name the relevant chemical species and the observed state.
Check which property distinguishes the candidate explanations.
Conserve each component while changing a condition; do not assume the conclusion.

core1b.predict: Make an initial classification or qualitative prediction and state one condition it depends upon.
core1b.attempt: A mixture contains sand, sodium chloride and water. Devise a sequence to isolate sand, water and salt.
core1b.reconstruct: Rebuild the solution by comparing each candidate model against the observations and conservation rules.
core1b.diagnose: Which observation would expose the incorrect route: One universal filter can remove both sand grains and dissolved ions?
core1b.repair: Match each operation to particle size or volatility; preserve each component.
core1b.boundary: Would the same route recover volatile ethanol from an ethanol-water mixture unchanged?
core1b.model_response: Filter first to collect insoluble sand, wash/dry it; distil filtrate to collect water; crystallise/dry residual salt. Quantify losses and purity as separate checks.

subtopics.source_notes: Class IX separation principles and simple apparatus.

deep_dive.big_idea: A separation method is not a name to memorise in isolation. It is a controlled physical process that creates different paths for components: nonvolatile salt remains while water vaporises; crystal solute may precipitate on cooling; different dye components migrate at different rates in chromatography.
reasoning_path: List every component and whether it is dissolved, suspended, volatile or likely to react under proposed conditions.
Choose the property contrast: filtration for large insoluble particles, distillation for volatility, crystallisation for solubility, chromatography for partition behaviour.
Sketch the apparatus and label where each component moves; a product missing from the drawing signals an incomplete mass balance.
Check recovery and purity separately. Collecting clear distillate is not itself proof of absolute chemical purity.

discovery.title: Recover the water and the salt
discovery.setup: Imagine laboratory brine in a correctly designed teacher-operated distillation apparatus connected to a condenser and receiver.
discovery.predict: Where should the salt and the water end up if no spray entrainment or side reaction occurs?
discovery.observation: Water vapour condenses into a receiver while the nonvolatile salt remains in the heated vessel or residue.
discovery.interpretation: Volatility, followed by condensation, enables recovery of a liquid separately from dissolved nonvolatile matter.
discovery.limits: Heating apparatus needs trained supervision; volatile impurities and droplets may contaminate the collected liquid.

deep_dive.connection: Some mixtures defeat ordinary filtration or distillation and require another property contrast or a staged route.

subtopics.title: Separation: centrifugation, sublimation and coagulation
subtopics.entry_question: If ordinary filtering fails to remove tiny suspended particles, what other physical distinction can we exploit?
core1a_paragraphs: Centrifugation accelerates sedimentation of dispersed components that differ in density and size under suitable conditions. It changes separation rate, not chemical identity. A centrifuge does not separate every molecule merely by spinning.

Sublimation occurs when a solid enters the gas phase without passing through an ordinary bulk liquid phase under specified conditions; substances such as iodine may be separated from non-subliming mixtures in some classroom demonstrations.

Coagulation deliberately destabilises certain colloids, causing small dispersed particles to aggregate into larger structures that may settle or filter. The process must be chemically appropriate to the dispersion and its conditions.
subtopics.representation: Provide three sketches with arrows: spin tubes with sediment, subliming solid to cold surface, colloidal small clusters to larger flocs. Each figure labels which property differences are exploited.

worked_example.problem: An ink-like colloidal suspension passes ordinary filter paper. Name a possible next method and why it may help.
steps: Identify that the dispersed particles are too small for ordinary filtration.
Consider coagulation if the colloid can be destabilised safely, forming larger aggregates.
Filter or settle the resulting aggregates.
Check whether the treatment changes the chemical analyte of interest.
worked_example.result: Coagulation followed by settling/filtration is one candidate route.
worked_example.check: A separation strategy must preserve what is meant to be recovered.

misconception.wrong: All suspensions and colloids can be separated by the same filter paper.
misconception.why: Particle size and dispersion stability vary widely.
misconception.repair: State the separation mechanism and its material/size limitations.

demands.title: Acceleration and sedimentation
demands.core1a_explanation: Centrifugation exploits different response of dispersed particles to an applied acceleration field.
demands.worked_reasoning: A centrifuge can pellet cells or insoluble particulates while some small dissolved molecules remain in the supernatant.
demands.independent_check: Compare particle scale and density contrast.
hints: Name the relevant chemical species and the observed state.
Check which property distinguishes the candidate explanations.
Conserve each component while changing a condition; do not assume the conclusion.

core1b.predict: Make an initial classification or qualitative prediction and state one condition it depends upon.
core1b.attempt: Why might a centrifuge separate fine solid particles faster than leaving a tube on a bench?
core1b.reconstruct: Rebuild the solution by comparing each candidate model against the observations and conservation rules.
core1b.diagnose: Which observation would expose the incorrect route: A centrifuge destroys or changes the particles into a solid residue?
core1b.repair: Explain differential movement without changing species identity.
core1b.boundary: Would a perfectly homogeneous molecular solution necessarily form a pellet?
core1b.model_response: The strong effective acceleration increases the tendency of density-different particles to move relative to liquid, often speeding sedimentation. Dissolved molecules are not automatically pelleted.

demands.title: Select sublimation or filtration
demands.core1a_explanation: Choosing separation requires knowing whether the relevant components are insoluble or volatile under accessible conditions.
demands.worked_reasoning: A solid mixture containing a subliming component can sometimes be heated gently and condensed on a cool surface.
demands.independent_check: Identify the recovered component's phase trajectory.
hints: Name the relevant chemical species and the observed state.
Check which property distinguishes the candidate explanations.
Conserve each component while changing a condition; do not assume the conclusion.

core1b.predict: Make an initial classification or qualitative prediction and state one condition it depends upon.
core1b.attempt: A solid mixture contains iodine and sand. Propose a simple principle for separating iodine and explain the essential apparatus feature.
core1b.reconstruct: Rebuild the solution by comparing each candidate model against the observations and conservation rules.
core1b.diagnose: Which observation would expose the incorrect route: Every solid in the mixture evaporates at the same temperature?
core1b.repair: Use different phase-change tendencies and a cool deposition surface.
core1b.boundary: Would simply dissolving both in water have the same selective effect?
core1b.model_response: Under controlled conditions iodine can sublime to vapour and deposit on a cool surface while sand remains. Ventilation and safety controls are needed.

demands.title: Combine treatment and mechanical separation
demands.core1a_explanation: Some colloids are not filterable until particles aggregate; combining a chemical destabilisation step with filtration is a dependent sequence.
demands.worked_reasoning: Coagulation can enlarge small particles; the following filtration becomes effective only after aggregation.
demands.independent_check: Check clarified sample purity and treatment residue.
hints: Name the relevant chemical species and the observed state.
Check which property distinguishes the candidate explanations.
Conserve each component while changing a condition; do not assume the conclusion.

core1b.predict: Make an initial classification or qualitative prediction and state one condition it depends upon.
core1b.attempt: A stable colloidal sample passes filter paper but must be clarified. Justify the order 'coagulate then filter' rather than the reverse.
core1b.reconstruct: Rebuild the solution by comparing each candidate model against the observations and conservation rules.
core1b.diagnose: Which observation would expose the incorrect route: Repeating the failed filtration infinitely many times is sufficient?
core1b.repair: Identify the bottleneck and modify particle size before mechanical separation.
core1b.boundary: What if the coagulating agent remains dissolved in the filtrate?
core1b.model_response: The initial particles pass the filter. Coagulation first produces larger aggregates that the subsequent filter can retain. The order matters, and the treatment must be chosen for the actual colloid.

subtopics.source_notes: Core separation awareness; practical suitability and safety require local supervision.

deep_dive.big_idea: A separation sometimes becomes possible only after a preparatory step changes particle size or physical state. Coagulation helps some colloids aggregate; centrifugation accelerates sedimentation; sublimation allows a substance to travel through the vapour phase and deposit elsewhere.
reasoning_path: Identify why the first straightforward technique fails: dissolved ions and many colloids pass ordinary filter paper.
Choose a physically justified intervention—aggregation for colloids, enhanced sedimentation for dense particles, selective sublimation for suitable solids.
Order the steps so that the property contrast used by the final separator actually exists when that separator operates.
Account for residual reagents, trapped product and safety limitations; a recovered solid may not be chemically pure.

discovery.title: Why the order of operations matters
discovery.setup: A hypothetical stable colloid passes through ordinary filter paper, while a suitable controlled coagulant is known to form larger aggregates.
discovery.predict: Would filtering first and then adding coagulant recover as much dispersed matter as coagulating before filtration?
discovery.observation: The filter initially cannot retain the smallest dispersed particles; aggregation before filtration can create retainable clusters.
discovery.interpretation: Separation design is a causal sequence, not just a list of methods.
discovery.limits: The chosen coagulant must be compatible with the sample and may itself introduce soluble impurities.

deep_dive.connection: C03 shifts attention from physically separating substances to the atomic identities and chemical formulas that describe them.

chapter_spine.central_question: How can a sample look uniform while containing several substances—and how can we prove which separation will work?
prior_knowledge: Recognising substances by chemical identity, not appearance
Mass and volume measurement with appropriate units
journey: Describe solutions, suspensions and colloids across scales
Read solubility as a conditional equilibrium quantity
Design staged separations using particle or phase differences
chapter_spine.chapter_closure: The right separation method depends on a measured property difference. Decide which component changes phase, migrates, settles, scatters light or remains dissolved, and verify where each component ends up.

key_terms.mixture: Two or more substances combined without a fixed chemical combining ratio.
key_terms.solute: A component dissolved in a solution.
key_terms.solvent: The medium in which a solute dissolves.
key_terms.concentration: Amount of solute per specified amount of solution or solvent.
key_terms.solubility: Equilibrium maximum dissolved amount at stated temperature and pressure.
key_terms.chromatography: Separation using unequal distribution between mobile and stationary phases.
